members.title: Netanyahu, at risk of losing power, steps up attacks on Israel’s Arab parties
members.lead: Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu alleged on Thursday, without providing evidence, that Arab parties’ record gains in an election this week were driven in part by voter fraud, a charge rejected by Arab leaders who accused the premier of incitement. The allegation represents an escalation of rhetoric against Arab parties by Netanyahu and his far-right partners after high Arab turnout in a national ballot on Tuesday effectively blocked a smooth path to power for either him or his main rivals. Israeli officials said on Thursday that the authorities were probing fraud allegations, though the election’s integrity was not systematically compromised. . Analysts and critics say that by stepping up attacks on Arab parties, Netanyahu may be trying to ensure his main rival, Gadi Eisenkot, feels unable to even consider forming a minority government with Arab help that could oust him from power. Netanyahu’s goal is “delegitimising any Arab-Jewish cooperation”, said Eytan Gilboa, professor of politics at Reichman University. Tuesday’s tightly fought election has produced no clear winner and is likely to be followed by weeks of protracted negotiations over a new government. With nearly 99% of votes counted, Netanyahu’s nationalist-religious bloc held a modest lead in seats over a bloc of right-wing and centre-left parties led by Eisenkot, with both men’s coalitions short of the 61 seats needed for a majority in parliament. . Parties representing Israel’s 21% Arab minority were projected to win an unprecedented 19 seats, leaving Eisenkot’s bloc, which has 48 seats against Netanyahu’s camp of 53, with no path to power without broad Arab backing. Eisenkot has so far ruled out including the parties in government but his camp could try to form a minority government with Arab support from the outside. members.title: Friday briefing: Israel has a dilemma - can its opposition govern with Palestinian parties?
members.lead: In today’s newsletter: Benjamin Netanyahu has been left without a majority, now it is up to the coalition to find out whether the desire for change will prove to be a defining political moment Good morning. It was described by many Israelis as the most consequential election in their country’s history. And, as the final votes were tallied, it has delivered a result that presents Israel with a significant dilemma. Benjamin Netanyahu’s far-right coalition has lost its mandate while the opposition has a clear majority: but only if the Jewish Israeli opposition bloc, led by retired general Gadi Eisenkot, is prepared to make a governing pact with Palestinian Israeli parties, which have secured a historic result. members.title: With no majority, what options remain for Israel's Netanyahu, Eisenkot?
members.lead: Following elections in which Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and his main rival Gadi Eisenkot both fell short of a majority, each is claiming a mandate to govern -- though neither has explained how. Given the indecisive result, the two leaders would need to find a way to broaden their blocs if they hope to secure a governing coalition, but so far very little information has leaked about potential behind-the-scenes negotiations. If neither succeeds in securing a coalition, the country will have to head back to the polls. AFP looks at the most plausible scenarios for each side forming a government. .Netanyahu, at risk of losing power, steps up attacks on Israel’s Arab parties. The prime minister and his far-right and ultra-Orthodox allies came out ahead in the final vote count, with 53 seats in parliament, including 27 for the premier's party, Likud. But that is still short of the 61 needed for a majority. If he hopes to stay in power, Netanyahu will have to reach out to opposition parties with a pitch to join his government -- a major about-face after a campaign run on vows to unseat him. Israeli President Isaac Herzog, who is tasked with tapping the candidate best positioned to form a coalition, has said a new vote must be avoided at all costs. Of the four parties in Eisenkot's camp, the least receptive to an overture from Netanyahu would be the left-wing Democrats, led by Yair Golan, which won eight seats. Netanyahu's former ally turned fierce critic Avigdor Lieberman, whose right-wing Yisrael Beiteinu party won seven seats, would also likely dismiss the prospect out of hand. . Lieberman said on Thursday that "the only conceivable coalition" was one without Netanyahu, though he suggested the rest of the premier's party would be tolerated. The stance of Naftali Bennett's centre-right Together party, which won 12 seats, is less clear.
